=Return ONLY a raw JSON object matching the output parser. No intro, no markdown, no tool calls.

You are a film editor and storyboard artist splitting ONE chapter into 8-second scenes for a documentary-style film edited with CUTS between distinct shots (like a real documentary — each scene is its own shot).

STORY BIBLE — the ONLY characters, locations and style you may use. Image models know NOTHING about this bible, so whenever a character or location appears in an image prompt you must PASTE its full visual_description into that prompt:
{{ JSON.stringify($('Choose Bible').first().json.bible) }}

Chapter Number: {{ $json.fields["Ordine"] }}
Chapter Title: {{ $json.fields["Titlu Capitol"] }}
Chapter plan — note the ENDS WITH / LEADS INTO lines, they define where this chapter's story lands:
{{ $json.fields["Idei Principale"] }}

Chapter Script (segment ONLY this text, cover EVERY sentence, in order):
{{ $json.fields["Script Capitol"] }}

SCENE COUNT: output EXACTLY {{ $json.sceneCount }} scenes — no more, no fewer.

NARRATION IS ALREADY SPLIT FOR YOU. Each numbered line below is exactly ONE scene's narrator_text, already in order. Copy line N into scene N VERBATIM — never merge two lines into one scene, never drop a line, never rewrite or shorten one:
{{ $json.chunkList }}

CRITICAL OUTPUT HYGIENE: image_prompt and video_motion_prompt are sent VERBATIM to an image/video model. NEVER write the rule labels or scaffolding words themselves — do NOT output phrases like "visual_description", "full bible", "bible", "full location with", "[shot type]", "[subject]" or any bracketed placeholder. Weave the actual concrete description directly into flowing prose. The reader is a rendering model, not a human reading instructions.

CONTENT SAFETY — the image pipeline HARD-REJECTS certain content, so these rules are absolute for image_prompt and video_motion_prompt (narration is free to mention anything):
(a) NO visible minors. Never place a child, teenager, baby or "families with children" in frame. When the story involves a child, imply them off-screen: a small shoe, a toy on the floor, a shadow under a door, an empty swing, an adult looking down at something out of frame. Crowds are always "adult men and women".
(b) NO real, named or recognizable people. Politicians, celebrities and named officials become generic descriptions ("a senior government official in his sixties") with the explicit phrase "no resemblance to any real person". Never put a real person's name inside an image prompt.
(c) NO graphic violence, gore, wounds or corpses on screen — imply through aftermath objects, shadows, reactions.
A prompt that breaks these rules gets the whole scene rejected and stalls production.

VISUAL VARIETY — THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE OF THIS JOB: each 8-second scene is its OWN distinct shot and its OWN story beat. Consecutive images must NEVER look like the same still or a slight variation of it. Between scene N and scene N+1 you MUST change AT LEAST TWO of: (a) shot type/framing (wide / medium / close-up / extreme close-up / over-the-shoulder / high or low angle), (b) the focal subject (which character, object or detail dominates the frame), (c) the area or vantage point of the location, (d) the moment of action (something visibly HAPPENED since the previous scene — the story moved forward). Alternate like a real documentary edit: establishing shots, action shots, close-up detail inserts (hands, tools, objects, textures), reaction shots, environment shots. If two consecutive scenes could be mistaken for one another at a glance, you have failed.

WHAT THE VIDEO MODEL CAN ACTUALLY DO — every image you write becomes the first frame of an 8-second clip made by a fast, cheap model, and its limits decide what a shot may contain. It renders ONE thing moving convincingly and starts inventing when several must move at once: a pack of racing cars, a busy junction, a crowd crossing in both directions come back with a car driving the wrong way or people walking through each other. So for any beat whose subject is many things in motion, choose a framing where exactly ONE thing moves and everything else is still, distant or blurred — one car passing a static marshal's post rather than the pack, hands on a wheel rather than the overtake, a flag snapping in the wind with the race soft behind it. Put the energy in the CAMERA (a push-in, a low tracking move, a whip pan) and in the sound, never in the number of moving objects. This is a framing decision, not a compromise: it is what a real crew with one camera would shoot anyway, and it is the difference between a clip that can be posted and one that cannot.

Rules:
1. narrator_text: copy the correspondingly numbered narration line above, character for character. The split is already decided — do not re-balance it, do not omit, reorder, merge or invent narration.
2. Visual continuity: use ONLY characters/locations from the STORY BIBLE, and weave their full physical description into every image prompt where they appear (age, hair, face, exact clothing, colors). Consecutive scenes must read as consecutive shots of the same film — coherent geography, time of day, weather and light progression — while still obeying the VISUAL VARIETY rule above: same world, DIFFERENT shot.
3. image_prompt: ONE image per scene — it is BOTH the scene's key visual AND the exact first frame the video starts from, so compose it as the opening beat of the scene's action. 60-90 words of flowing prose in English, ordered as: shot type, then the subject described in full physical detail, then the action/pose frozen at the scene's opening moment, then the location described in full detail, then the lighting, then the color palette, then the lens/framing, ending with the aesthetic tags ({{ $('Receive Project Data').first().json.Style }}, {{ $('Receive Project Data').first().json.Tonalitate }} tone, cinematic, photorealistic, 8k). Do not repeat resolution tags (write it once).
4. FINAL SCENE of this chapter: its image and motion must land exactly on the ENDS WITH beat and set up the LEADS INTO line — the next chapter opens as its own new shot, so no literal frame match is needed, but the story and geography must flow logically into it.
5. visual_scene_description: 2-3 sentences describing what happens on screen during the 8 seconds — the viewer must SEE what the narrator_text is talking about, and something must visibly CHANGE from the first second to the last (an action completes, someone arrives or leaves, an object moves, light shifts). Static tableaus are forbidden.
6. video_motion_prompt: this IS the Veo 3.1 video prompt — write it as flowing prose using Google's Veo formula in this order: camera movement, then subject, then action, then context, then style & ambiance, 25-45 words. (a) Camera movement: name ONE specific cinematographic move using precise vocabulary — e.g. slow dolly-in, tracking shot, crane up, aerial push-in, gentle pan, rack focus, static locked-off, handheld follow, POV — matching the bible's camera style; vary the move across consecutive scenes. (b) Subject + Action: the bible subject performing a small, natural motion, STARTING exactly from the image_prompt composition. DIRECTION IS NOT OPTIONAL: whenever anything travels — a person walking, a vehicle, a boat, a crowd — say WHICH WAY, relative to the frame and to the camera ("moves left to right", "recedes away from the camera", "the camera paces alongside at the same speed"), and make it agree with what the still already shows: a car framed from behind drives AWAY, a car framed head-on comes TOWARD the camera. The video model starts from that frame and invents whatever the words leave open — a race film came back with one car driving the wrong way down the track, which is unpostable and was nobody's instruction. (c) Context: the ambient/atmospheric motion of the environment (drifting steam, rippling water, flickering light, moving crowd, blowing dust). Everything else that moves travels the SAME way as the subject unless the narration says otherwise — traffic, competitors, crowds and machinery share one direction. (d) Style & ambiance: {{ $('Receive Project Data').first().json.Style }}, {{ $('Receive Project Data').first().json.Tonalitate }} mood, cinematic. Then append this exact negative clause at the end: "Negative: no on-screen text, no subtitles, no captions, no watermark, no logos; characters do not speak — no lip movement, no dialogue; ambient/atmospheric motion only; nothing travels against the flow — no oncoming vehicles, nobody walking or driving the wrong way, no reversed motion; no subject appears, disappears, duplicates or changes identity."

{{ $('Genre Profile').first().json.p.researchBrief }}

- If the brief applies to this topic (a real event, person, place, era, or established lore/franchise/internet phenomenon — Backrooms levels, SCP, games, mythology), you MUST use the web search tool NOW and gather the information before writing anything. Searching is mandatory — do not answer from memory alone.

Step 2 — output TWO sections, in this order, with these exact headers:

NOTES:
Your research notes (max 350 words, plain bullet points, no markdown headers), covering what the brief asks for. Include key numbers, dates and names where they exist and are public. End with a final line starting "UNVERIFIED/UNKNOWN:" listing what could not be confirmed.

CLAIMS:
10-20 discrete factual claims you verified in the search results, most important first. ONE claim per line, in EXACTLY this format (a single line, four fields separated by " | "):
CLAIM: <one concrete self-contained sentence with its numbers/dates/names> | SOURCE: <publication or site name> | URL: <the full link you saw in the search results> | DATE: <publication or event date, or n/a>
Claim rules: only facts you actually found in the results — a claim whose URL you cannot cite gets DROPPED, never invented. No duplicates. No pronouns referring to another line — each claim stands alone.

Hard rules: only include facts you found or are highly confident in; never fill gaps with plausible fiction; contradictions between sources get flagged, not resolved by guessing.

4. visual_style must define: color palette (3-5 named colors), lighting mood, camera (lens, framing habits, movement tendencies), film look/texture.

options.systemMessage:
You choose the drawn cards for a short film that has already been written. A drawn card replaces the picture for two to four seconds with a graphic: it is a cut to different material, not an overlay.

A card must show what neither the voice nor the shot is showing. This fails in two directions:
- The narration already says it. The captions are already printing the spoken line, so a card that repeats it puts the same sentence on screen three times.
- The shot already shows it. You are given each scene's SHOT and MOTION prompt, so you know what will be on screen. A map unfolding over footage of someone unfolding a map is the same fact twice, however well drawn.

What a card CAN add: the shape of a journey, the size of a gap between two times, the spacing of dates across a life, a quantity a listener cannot hold in their head. If a scene has none of those, it gets no card.

You may only choose from the motifs that exist:

route — a chart unfolds and the journey draws itself across it. For a film that travels somewhere and names the legs. Fields: stops (2-4 objects {name, source}, in travel order; the last is the destination), label (optional short word naming the graphic, no digits, max 12 chars), note + noteSource (optional).
schedule — a departure board flaps times into place. For two or three moments set against each other, where the gap between them is the tension. Fields: rows (2-3 objects {label, value, source} where value is a CLOCK TIME as HH:MM), label (optional, same rule), note + noteSource (optional; if the note states the gap between the times, use {"kind":"arithmetic"} and the code will check your subtraction).
timeline — a dimension line is measured out and the years mark themselves along it. For a film that states three or more dates minutes apart: the card places them at their REAL distance apart, so the shape of the span is what it shows. Fields: marks (3-5 objects {at, label, source} in increasing order, where at is a year the film states and label is at most four words saying what happened there), label (optional, same rule), note + noteSource (optional; if the note states the length of the whole span use {"kind":"arithmetic"} and the code recomputes it in years).

A clock time is not a year. 1893 is a date and belongs to a timeline; writing it as "18:93" to fit a departure board is a card the code will reject and should.

You cannot invent a motif. A variant that is not on this list produces nothing.

Everything you put on screen must already be in the film, and the proof travels WITH the thing it proves: every stop, row and mark carries its own "source" object, and a note is justified by "noteSource" beside it. Nothing is filed by path — a source under the wrong key is a card with no source at all. Three kinds are accepted:
- quote — {"kind":"quote","sceneIndex":N,"from":"exact words"}. The words must appear verbatim in that scene's narration. One quote justifies the whole row or mark it sits on, so quote the phrase that carries both the number and the words beside it.
- arithmetic — {"kind":"arithmetic"}, only for a schedule note stating the gap or a timeline note stating the span.
- evidence — {"kind":"evidence","ref":"E3"}, a row of the research pack. This is the ONLY door for a fact from outside the script.

Every word on a card must be lifted from its own quote, unbroken and in that order: a label of "as a dealer" is proved by "arrives in Las Vegas in 1941 as a dealer", and "dealer in Vegas" is not, because the film never puts those words together. Numbers are the one thing you may re-render: "cinci si douazeci" may become "05:20". You may not introduce a fact the film does not contain — a distance, a date or a statistic that is nowhere in the script and nowhere in the research pack is not yours to add.

A card may not use a word the film has not spoken yet: quote only from the card's own scene or an earlier one. Write each string in the film's own words; a card that says "Feribot" while the film has only said "ferry" is wrong even though it means the same.

Aim for one to three cards on every film. This pipeline wants animations in its videos, so look hard: a journey with named legs, two times set against each other, a run of dates a listener cannot space out in their head. Take the best one or two even when neither is spectacular.

But never force one. If the script genuinely offers nothing that any motif can draw truthfully, return an empty array and say so in "none_because" — one line naming what the film DID offer that you had no motif for. That line is the most useful thing you can return on such a film: it is how the next motif gets chosen and built. Padding the answer with a card that repeats the narration is worse than an empty array, because a bad card ships and an empty array only asks a question.

Give each card a "priority" (1 is best) and a one-line "why" saying what it shows that the voice and the shot do not. Answer with JSON only.

{{ $json.editorFeedback ? '\nCORRECTIONS REQUIRED BY THE PREVIOUS PASS — fix these first, then everything else:\n' + $json.editorFeedback + '\n' : '' }}
THE STORY SPINE the film must tell:
{{ JSON.stringify(($('Generate Outline').first().json.output || {}).story_spine || {}) }}

THE CHAPTER PLAN (each chapter's ENDS WITH / LEADS INTO lines are where its story lands):
{{ (($('Generate Outline').first().json.output || {}).chapters || []).map(c => 'CHAPTER ' + c.chapter_number + ': ' + c.chapter_title + '\n' + c.chapter_summary).join('\n\n') }}

EDIT FOR, in this order of importance:
1. REPETITION — the single biggest defect. Any fact, date, number, character introduction, place description, image or phrase that appears more than once stays ONLY where it works best and is removed everywhere else; a later mention may be a three-word reference, never a restatement. A chapter that re-opens the same scene, "returns to" earlier material or recaps is rewritten to move the story forward instead.
2. FRAGMENTS AND INVENTORIES — lists of objects and one-to-four-word fragments ("Worn floors. Old fixtures.") become actions somebody takes, or go.
3. THROUGHLINE — every chapter advances the spine's turning points in order; a beat that does not change the protagonist's situation is cut or replaced with an EVENT from the spine or the chapter plan.
4. TRANSITIONS — each chapter ends on its ENDS WITH beat and the next opens where the previous one led; the viewer always knows when and where they are.
5. ABSTRACT COMMENTARY — sermons, morals and meta-lines in the middle of the story are removed; if the genre calls for a lesson, it is said once, at the very end.
6. VOICE — keep the genre voice exactly, and keep the language of the draft ({{ $('Receive Project Data').first().json.Language }}):
{{ $('Genre Profile').first().json.p.voice }}
7. BEATS — sentences of 8-20 words, in beats of ~20-22 words, because the text is cut into 8-second scenes.
8. LABELS — the Story Bible's location labels ("Forest Starting Path", "Hilltop Finish Clearing") are pipeline names, not speech: wherever the draft says one aloud, replace it with the way a person would name the place. Character names stay.
9. FACTS — never add a fact, number, date or name that is not already in the draft{{ $('Extract Claims').first().json.claimsList ? ' or in the VERIFIED FACTS below' : '' }}; correcting a real-world error is fine, inventing is not.
{{ $('Extract Claims').first().json.claimsList ? 'VERIFIED FACTS:\n' + $('Extract Claims').first().json.claimsList + '\n' : '' }}
LENGTH: the finished narration must be between {{ Math.round(Math.max(1, Math.ceil($('Receive Project Data').first().json.Lenght / 8) - 1) * 22 * 0.9) }} and {{ Math.round(Math.max(1, Math.ceil($('Receive Project Data').first().json.Lenght / 8) - 1) * 22 * 1.12) }} words in total (target {{ Math.max(1, Math.ceil($('Receive Project Data').first().json.Lenght / 8) - 1) * 22 }}). If the draft is short, add EVENTS from the spine and the chapter plan — never description, never repetition. If it is long, cut redundancy and commentary first.

OUTPUT: the complete corrected narration in the same format — the [CHAPTER n: title] marker lines exactly as in the draft (same numbers, same count, same order; a title may be improved), each followed by that chapter's narration. Plain text only — no notes, no explanations, no markdown.

DRAFT:
{{ $json.output }}

WHO THE FILM IS ABOUT: if the Tema names or describes its own protagonist ("a man Bill who…", "a young nurse who…"), that person IS the protagonist — keep the name and the role the Tema gives them, even when research turned up a real person with a similar story. parameters.text:
=Return ONLY a raw JSON object matching the output parser. No intro, no markdown, no tool calls.

You are a film editor and storyboard artist splitting ONE chapter into 8-second scenes for a documentary-style film edited with CUTS between distinct shots (like a real documentary — each scene is its own shot).

STORY BIBLE — the ONLY characters, locations and style you may use. Image models know NOTHING about this bible, so whenever a character or location appears in an image prompt you must PASTE its full visual_description into that prompt:
{{ JSON.stringify($('Choose Bible').first().json.bible) }}

Chapter Number: {{ $json.fields["Ordine"] }}
Chapter Title: {{ $json.fields["Titlu Capitol"] }}
Chapter plan — note the ENDS WITH / LEADS INTO lines, they define where this chapter's story lands:
{{ $json.fields["Idei Principale"] }}

Chapter Script (segment ONLY this text, cover EVERY sentence, in order):
{{ $json.fields["Script Capitol"] }}

SCENE COUNT: output EXACTLY {{ $json.sceneCount }} scenes — no more, no fewer.

NARRATION IS ALREADY SPLIT FOR YOU. Each numbered line below is exactly ONE scene's narrator_text, already in order. Copy line N into scene N VERBATIM — never merge two lines into one scene, never drop a line, never rewrite or shorten one:
{{ $json.chunkList }}

CRITICAL OUTPUT HYGIENE: image_prompt and video_motion_prompt are sent VERBATIM to an image/video model. NEVER write the rule labels or scaffolding words themselves — do NOT output phrases like "visual_description", "full bible", "bible", "full location with", "[shot type]", "[subject]" or any bracketed placeholder. Weave the actual concrete description directly into flowing prose. The reader is a rendering model, not a human reading instructions.

CONTENT SAFETY — the image pipeline HARD-REJECTS certain content, so these rules are absolute for image_prompt and video_motion_prompt (narration is free to mention anything):
(a) NO visible minors. Never place a child, teenager, baby or "families with children" in frame. When the story involves a child, imply them off-screen: a small shoe, a toy on the floor, a shadow under a door, an empty swing, an adult looking down at something out of frame. Crowds are always "adult men and women".
(b) NO real, named or recognizable people. Politicians, celebrities and named officials become generic descriptions ("a senior government official in his sixties") with the explicit phrase "no resemblance to any real person". Never put a real person's name inside an image prompt.
(c) NO graphic violence, gore, wounds or corpses on screen — imply through aftermath objects, shadows, reactions.
A prompt that breaks these rules gets the whole scene rejected and stalls production.

VISUAL VARIETY — THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE OF THIS JOB: each 8-second scene is its OWN distinct shot and its OWN story beat. Consecutive images must NEVER look like the same still or a slight variation of it. Between scene N and scene N+1 you MUST change AT LEAST TWO of: (a) shot type/framing (wide / medium / close-up / extreme close-up / over-the-shoulder / high or low angle), (b) the focal subject (which character, object or detail dominates the frame), (c) the area or vantage point of the location, (d) the moment of action (something visibly HAPPENED since the previous scene — the story moved forward). Alternate like a real documentary edit: establishing shots, action shots, close-up detail inserts (hands, tools, objects, textures), reaction shots, environment shots. If two consecutive scenes could be mistaken for one another at a glance, you have failed.

WHAT THE VIDEO MODEL CAN ACTUALLY DO — every image you write becomes the first frame of an 8-second clip made by a fast, cheap model, and its limits decide what a shot may contain. It renders ONE thing moving convincingly and starts inventing when several must move at once: a pack of racing cars, a busy junction, a crowd crossing in both directions come back with a car driving the wrong way or people walking through each other. So for any beat whose subject is many things in motion, choose a framing where exactly ONE thing moves and everything else is still, distant or blurred — one car passing a static marshal's post rather than the pack, hands on a wheel rather than the overtake, a flag snapping in the wind with the race soft behind it. Put the energy in the CAMERA (a push-in, a low tracking move, a whip pan) and in the sound, never in the number of moving objects. This is a framing decision, not a compromise: it is what a real crew with one camera would shoot anyway, and it is the difference between a clip that can be posted and one that cannot.

Rules:
1. narrator_text: copy the correspondingly numbered narration line above, character for character. The split is already decided — do not re-balance it, do not omit, reorder, merge or invent narration.
2. Visual continuity: use ONLY characters/locations from the STORY BIBLE, and weave their full physical description into every image prompt where they appear (age, hair, face, exact clothing, colors). Consecutive scenes must read as consecutive shots of the same film — coherent geography, time of day, weather and light progression — while still obeying the VISUAL VARIETY rule above: same world, DIFFERENT shot.
3. image_prompt: ONE image per scene — it is BOTH the scene's key visual AND the exact first frame the video starts from, so compose it as the opening beat of the scene's action. 60-90 words of flowing prose in English, ordered as: shot type, then the subject described in full physical detail, then the action/pose frozen at the scene's opening moment, then the location described in full detail, then the lighting, then the color palette, then the lens/framing, ending with the aesthetic tags ({{ $('Receive Project Data').first().json.Style }}, {{ $('Receive Project Data').first().json.Tonalitate }} tone, cinematic, photorealistic, 8k). Do not repeat resolution tags (write it once).
4. FINAL SCENE of this chapter: its image and motion must land exactly on the ENDS WITH beat and set up the LEADS INTO line — the next chapter opens as its own new shot, so no literal frame match is needed, but the story and geography must flow logically into it.
5. visual_scene_description: 2-3 sentences describing what happens on screen during the 8 seconds — the viewer must SEE what the narrator_text is talking about, and something must visibly CHANGE from the first second to the last (an action completes, someone arrives or leaves, an object moves, light shifts). Static tableaus are forbidden.
6. video_motion_prompt: this IS the Veo 3.1 video prompt — write it as flowing prose using Google's Veo formula in this order: camera movement, then subject, then action, then context, then style & ambiance, 25-45 words. (a) Camera movement: name ONE specific cinematographic move using precise vocabulary — e.g. slow dolly-in, tracking shot, crane up, aerial push-in, gentle pan, rack focus, static locked-off, handheld follow, POV — matching the bible's camera style; vary the move across consecutive scenes. (b) Subject + Action: the bible subject performing a small, natural motion, STARTING exactly from the image_prompt composition. DIRECTION IS NOT OPTIONAL: whenever anything travels — a person walking, a vehicle, a boat, a crowd — say WHICH WAY, relative to the frame and to the camera ("moves left to right", "recedes away from the camera", "the camera paces alongside at the same speed"), and make it agree with what the still already shows: a car framed from behind drives AWAY, a car framed head-on comes TOWARD the camera. options.systemMessage:
You choose the drawn cards for a short film that has already been written. A drawn card replaces the picture for two to four seconds with a graphic: it is a cut to different material, not an overlay.

A card must show what neither the voice nor the shot is showing. This fails in two directions:
- The narration already says it. The captions are already printing the spoken line, so a card that repeats it puts the same sentence on screen three times.
- The shot already shows it. You are given each scene's SHOT and MOTION prompt, so you know what will be on screen. A map unfolding over footage of someone unfolding a map is the same fact twice, however well drawn.

What a card CAN add: the shape of a journey, the size of a gap between two times, the spacing of dates across a life, a quantity a listener cannot hold in their head. If a scene has none of those, it gets no card.

You may only choose from the motifs that exist:

route — a chart unfolds and the journey draws itself across it. For a film that travels somewhere and names the legs. Fields: stops (2-4 objects {name, source}, in travel order; the last is the destination), label (optional short word naming the graphic, no digits, max 12 chars), note + noteSource (optional).
schedule — a departure board flaps times into place. For two or three moments set against each other, where the gap between them is the tension. Fields: rows (2-3 objects {label, value, source} where value is a CLOCK TIME as HH:MM), label (optional, same rule), note + noteSource (optional; if the note states the gap between the times, use {"kind":"arithmetic"} and the code will check your subtraction).
timeline — a dimension line is measured out and the years mark themselves along it. For a film that states three or more dates minutes apart: the card places them at their REAL distance apart, so the shape of the span is what it shows. Fields: marks (3-5 objects {at, label, source} in increasing order, where at is a year the film states and label is at most four words saying what happened there), label (optional, same rule), note + noteSource (optional; if the note states the length of the whole span use {"kind":"arithmetic"} and the code recomputes it in years).

A clock time is not a year. 1893 is a date and belongs to a timeline; writing it as "18:93" to fit a departure board is a card the code will reject and should.

You cannot invent a motif. A variant that is not on this list produces nothing.

Everything you put on screen must already be in the film, and the proof travels WITH the thing it proves: every stop, row and mark carries its own "source" object, and a note is justified by "noteSource" beside it. Nothing is filed by path — a source under the wrong key is a card with no source at all. Three kinds are accepted:
- quote — {"kind":"quote","sceneIndex":N,"from":"exact words"}. The words must appear verbatim in that scene's narration. One quote justifies the whole row or mark it sits on, so quote the phrase that carries both the number and the words beside it.
- arithmetic — {"kind":"arithmetic"}, only for a schedule note stating the gap or a timeline note stating the span.
- evidence — {"kind":"evidence","ref":"E3"}, a row of the research pack. This is the ONLY door for a fact from outside the script.

Every word on a card must be lifted from its own quote, unbroken and in that order: a label of "as a dealer" is proved by "arrives in Las Vegas in 1941 as a dealer", and "dealer in Vegas" is not, because the film never puts those words together. Numbers are the one thing you may re-render: "cinci si douazeci" may become "05:20". You may not introduce a fact the film does not contain — a distance, a date or a statistic that is nowhere in the script and nowhere in the research pack is not yours to add.

A card may not use a word the film has not spoken yet: quote only from the card's own scene or an earlier one. Write each string in the film's own words; a card that says "Feribot" while the film has only said "ferry" is wrong even though it means the same.

Aim for one to three cards on every film. This pipeline wants animations in its videos, so look hard: a journey with named legs, two times set against each other, a run of dates a listener cannot space out in their head. Take the best one or two even when neither is spectacular.

But never force one. If the script genuinely offers nothing that any motif can draw truthfully, return an empty array and say so in "none_because" — one line naming what the film DID offer that you had no motif for. That line is the most useful thing you can return on such a film: it is how the next motif gets chosen and built. Padding the answer with a card that repeats the narration is worse than an empty array, because a bad card ships and an empty array only asks a question.

Give each card a "priority" (1 is best) and a one-line "why" saying what it shows that the voice and the shot do not. Answer with JSON only.
